title: A child's first practice
hookLine: the Buddha's son Rahula sits under a tree; Sariputta says practice the breath, and that evening Rahula asks his father how
tomorrow: why does a stranger on the road ask, 'What things?'

cards: Just breathe, someone tells a crying kid, and as an order, it doesn't land. The suttas tell how the Buddha's own son was taught. One morning Rahula walks behind his father on the alms round in the city of Savatthi.
The Buddha turns and gives him a short teaching: this body is not mine. Rahula doesn't go on for food. He turns back, sits down under a tree, legs crossed, back straight.
Sariputta, a senior monk, finds him there and says: Rahula, practice mindfulness of breathing; it bears great fruit. That evening Rahula goes to his father and asks: how?

teach.b: You might expect the Buddha to start with the breath. He starts with the ground. Be like the earth, Rahula, he says.
People throw clean things and dirty things on the earth, and it isn't troubled by any of it. Be like that, and pleasant and unpleasant things won't take over your mind.
Then be like water, which washes clean and dirty things alike.
Then like fire, like wind, like open space.
Then a few practices of the heart.
And at last the breath: sit down, back straight, and simply know it. Breathing in long, you know you're breathing in long; breathing in short, you know you're breathing in short.
That is anapanasati, mindfulness of breathing, the breath practice the suttas teach, and here it is a father answering his son. Notice how it was handed on. Rahula asked first.

His father didn't order a breath; he gave him something steady to stand on, and then a breath to know, not to fix. For a child in a hard moment, that's a different thing from just breathe. Feet on the floor.
The ground holding you, whatever has been thrown at it today. Then one breath, noticed together.

how: Buddhists practice mindfulness of breathing, anapanasati, knowing each breath without forcing it; parents who borrow the Rahula story start a child with feet on the ground and one easy breath.

games.q: what does “a child's first practice” mean?
o: a first prayer, learned by heart at bedtime
a first, easy practice: noticing one breath at ease
a strict daily routine an adult sets for a child

p: sat under a tree instead of going for food
untroubled by clean or dirty things
knowing the breath, not forcing it

s: the Buddha taught his son the breath by telling him to calm down
the popular picture of 'just breathe'. Rahula asked how, and his father began with the earth.
in the sutta, Sariputta is the one who first tells Rahula to practice the breath
that evening Rahula went to his father and asked how.
the Buddha told Rahula to be like the earth, untroubled by clean or dirty things
then water, fire, wind and space, and later the breath.

games.q: your sister sets a ten-minute meditation timer for her six-year-old every night, and he hates it. what fits the Rahula story?
o: start with feet on the floor and one easy breath, and let him ask for more.
keep the ten minutes; discipline now makes it easier later on.
drop it for now; small kids can't do anything like meditation.
games.why: Rahula asked first, and his father gave him the steady earth before the breath. the practice was answered, not imposed.

practice: Put both feet flat on the floor, or your hands flat on the chair, and feel the ground holding you up, the way the Buddha told Rahula to be like the earth.
Then notice one breath, from the start of the in-breath to the end of the out-breath. Don't change it; just know it. When you lose it, feel the ground again and begin with the next one.

wordCard.voice: A child's first practice: as the Buddha gave it to his son, something steady to stand on first, then one breath, known, not ordered.

orig.note: Pali, written in Devanagari: mindfulness of breathing in and out, the breath practice the Buddha taught.

carryVoice: Keep this: one breath, on steady ground, the way the Buddha answered Rahula. Rest well.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 62 (Maha-Rahulovada Sutta): the alms round in Savatthi; 'this is not mine'; Rahula sits under a tree; Sariputta: develop mindfulness of breathing; the Buddha teaches meditation like earth, water, fire, air and space, the practices of the heart, then mindfulness of breathing ('breathing in long, he knows I breathe in long')
